title: And yes, by the way, for all the thorny ethics around bootlegs, it’s ...
transcript: One of the common arguments against bootlegs and pro shots in theatre that kind of bothers me is when people are like “oh, but theatre is meant to be experienced LIVE!” I agree with that as a statement on its own, and I agree with it when it comes to dismissing a show solely because you saw a bootleg. But I really disagree with it as an argument against any sort of video preservation of theatrical productions. People like to romanticize the ephemeral nature of theatre, and for a reason. Like, of course, there's something beautiful to the way we experience this thing in a room together that only happens exactly the same way once. But I think what gets lost sometimes in that romanticization is that theatre isn't just an experience, it's an art form. These are individual works of art that people put a lot of time and effort into. And just because theatre doesn't reflexively preserve itself the way that other art forms do, doesn't mean that you *shouldn't* do it if the option is available. You wouldn't say a blockbuster movie deserves to be discarded entirely just because it's better if you experience it in a cinema. And if, for example, a playwright has a story to tell, there are other artistic reasons to choose theatre as your medium that have nothing to do with the fact that it's gonna disappear when you're done. And just because there's a certain X factor, like an intangible Aura to the live experience that can never be perfectly captured on camera doesn't mean that the rest of it can't be. And I'd argue that “the rest of it” actually makes up the vast majority of the contents of a theatrical production, not least of which is, like, the story like the emotions, themes, whatever that's conveyed in the text. And you might say that you could get that from a script or a cast recording if it's a musical, but there's still a lot of in between content that can't be conveyed on the page but can be captured on camera, especially like most of the interpretive choices that the director and actors make. And at least a version of the staging, design, choreography, etc. Even if it's not like the full picture, you can still reach a certain critical mass that makes it well worth it. And of course, there are logistical and financial difficulties to making pro shots widely available. But that's not what I'm talking about. And of course, there are valid arguments against bootlegs and valid arguments against the sense of entitlement that a lot of theatre fans have, but emphasising this romantic notion of theatre as something that is supposed to disappear is, for me at least, not one of them.
